record.paper_title: Open problems in dynamics and related fields
record.original_question: Can periodic orbits be constructed for triangular billiards?

evidence.quote: QUESTION 29 (A. Katok). Construct periodic orbits for triangular billiards.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider billiard dynamics in a triangle $T \subset \mathbb{R}^2$: a point particle moves in straight lines inside $T$ and reflects off the boundary according to the law of equal angles (the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection), with the dynamics left undefined when the trajectory hits a vertex. A trajectory is called a periodic orbit if, after finitely many reflections, the particle returns to its initial position with its initial direction.

Problem: Prove that every triangle $T$ admits a periodic billiard orbit. Equivalently, give a construction that, for an arbitrary triangle $T$ (including arbitrary obtuse triangles), produces at least one periodic billiard trajectory in $T$.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of constructing a periodic orbit in every triangle remains open in general. Periodic orbits exist trivially in right and acute triangles (e.g., the Fagnano orbit). For obtuse triangles, R. Schwartz proved existence whenever the largest angle is at most 100°, later extended via rigorous computer-assisted search by Schwartz and Tokarsky to triangles with maximum angle up to roughly 112.3°. The case of arbitrary obtuse triangles, especially with very large maximum angle, is still open.

status_evidence.title: Triangular billiards - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Whether every triangle has a periodic billiards path is a long-standing open problem. Periodic orbits are known to exist on all nonobtuse and certain classes of obtuse triangles.
status_evidence.claim: Existence of a periodic billiard orbit in every triangle is a long-standing open problem.

status_evidence.title: Obtuse Triangular Billiards II: One Hundred Degrees Worth of Periodic Orbits
status_evidence.snippet: Every obtuse triangle with largest angle at most 100 degrees has a periodic billiard path.
status_evidence.claim: Schwartz proved periodic orbits exist for obtuse triangles with maximum angle ≤ 100°.

status_evidence.title: Obtuse Billiards (Tokarsky et al.)
status_evidence.snippet: Rigorous computer search extends existence of periodic orbits to obtuse triangles with maximum angle up to about 112.3°.
status_evidence.claim: The known range has been extended beyond 100° but the full conjecture is still open.
